body.heading: A routine that protects you
paragraphs: Roads are for cars, and cars are big, fast and cannot stop instantly. But children cross roads safely every day — by using a routine so simple you can say it in your sleep: Stop. Look. Listen. Think. Walk.
Learn the words here. Practice the real thing only with a grown-up holding your hand or close beside you.

body.heading: Stop and look
paragraphs: STOP — Stop at the curb, before the road begins. Never step off the curb while you are still deciding.

LOOK — Look left, look right, then look left again. (In countries where cars drive on the left, it is right, left, right — ask your grown-up which way your country starts.) Look for cars, bicycles, buses — and remember that quiet electric cars are easy to miss.

body.heading: Listen and think
paragraphs: LISTEN — Ears catch what eyes miss: engines, sirens, bicycle bells. No headphones, no phone, no game while crossing — your ears are safety tools.
THINK — Is anything coming? Is that parked car hiding a moving one? Can drivers see ME? If you are not sure, wait. Waiting is always allowed.

body.heading: Walk — don't run
paragraphs: WALK straight across, still looking as you go. Running makes you trip and makes you harder to predict. Use a marked crossing or a crossing guard when there is one — they exist to be used.
And one more: never chase a ball, a dog or anything else into a road. Things can be replaced. You cannot be. Let it go and tell a grown-up.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Say the routine out loud three times: Stop, Look, Listen, Think, Walk. Can you say it backwards? (You do not need to — but it is fun.)
2. Why does the chart say parked cars can be dangerous even though they are not moving?

takeaway: Stop at the curb, look left-right-left, listen with unplugged ears, think, then walk — never run, never chase anything into a road.
materials: Just you and this page for learning the words — real practice needs a grown-up and a quiet street
supervision: An adult must practice real crossings with the child, holding hands with younger children. This page teaches the routine only.
safetyNotes: Never practice crossing alone — an adult is always present for real-road practice.
No phones, headphones or games while crossing: ears and eyes are the safety tools.
Never chase a ball, pet or any object into a road; tell a grown-up instead.
screenFreeExtension: Practice the routine on a walk with your grown-up: say each step out loud at every curb, even the tiny quiet ones.
